newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Justice Department tobacco probe to go ahead.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Justice Department tobacco probe to go ahead.

text.p: Justice Department officials said on Friday their broad investigation of major cigarette companies would proceed, largely unaffected by the historic agreement between the tobacco industry and state negotiators.

They said the wide-ranging criminal probe would go forward despite the tentative settlement that requires tobacco firms to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to compensate the states and smokers, and to submit to tough new government regulation.

"What happens in that settlement is not binding on us," one official said. Other sources said participants made clear to the tobacco firms in the first negotiating sessions that the Justice Department would not participate in any agreement.

Justice Department prosecutors from the fraud section, assisted by FBI agents, have been investigating allegations the tobacco industry and its top executives withheld information and lied to Congress and federal agencies.

The officials emphasised that any decision on bringing criminal charges would not be influenced by the settlement, which still must be approved by the White House and Congress. "The charges are there or they aren't. That is the only thing we are concerned with," one official said.
The investigation is specifically examining allegations the heads of the major cigarette companies committed perjury when they testified before Congress in 1994 that nicotine was not addictive.

There are also a number of other tobacco-related probes by the Justice Department, including one in New York probing the industry for securities fraud. A grand jury is considering whether tobacco companies deceived shareholders about what they knew about the health risks of smoking.

The officials declined to predict when indictments might be returned, saying they were unaware of any timetable. But other sources closely following the investigation said there may be charges later this year.
The Justice Department already is reviewing the internal documents from Liggett Group Inc., which agreed to make them available as part of an earlier settlement with the state attorney generals.
The officials said the Justice Department will be waiting to see if more documents from other companies become available as part of the settlement.
